# AuraLite OS — Filesystem Performance (`filesystems_perf.md`)

**Generated by:** `tests/integration/cases/test_fsbench.sh` (the in-guest
lane) and `tests/unit/test_fsbench.c` (the host lane).
**Measurement date:** 2026-11-22, FSMODERN_PLAN.md **M0**.
**Baseline commit:** `bcc248f` + HOME_PLAN H0.

> This file is the answer to a question the tree could not answer before M0:
> **how fast is the storage?** Until now the answer was a sentence. Now it is
> a table, and the table is allowed to be unflattering.

---

## 1. What is measured, and on what

**Hardware.** `qemu-system-x86_64`, TCG (no KVM), 512 MiB RAM, 4 vCPUs,
AHCI with one 64 MiB raw image. These are **emulated** devices: the numbers
describe *this tree's software stack* (VFS → buffer cache → blkdev → AHCI →
QEMU), not a physical SSD. They are comparable **to each other and to later
runs of the same lane**, which is what a ratchet needs.

**Clock.** TSC, calibrated against `CLOCK_MONOTONIC` for 20 ms at startup.
The receipt says `clock=tsc`; if a machine has no usable TSC the tool falls
back to the 99 Hz kernel tick and **says so**, because a 10 ms clock cannot
time a 1 ms run.

**Workload.** `fsbench --dir X --files N --size 4096`:
create N files → write 4 KiB into each → `sync()` → read every file back and
**verify the bytes** → unlink all. The verification is not decoration: a
benchmark that does not check its payload measures a filesystem that may be
returning garbage quickly.

---

## 2. The numbers (2026-11-22, M0 baseline)

### tmpfs — `/tmp` (in memory)

| Metric | Value |
|---|---|
| seq_write | **16.98 MiB/s** |
| seq_read | **36.55 MiB/s** |
| create | **4 348 ops/s** |
| unlink | **28 070 ops/s** |
| sync | **1 303 µs** |
| payload | 8 × 4 KiB = 32 KiB, verified |

### `/fat` after M2 — the block layer change (AHCI, 64 MiB disk)

| Metric | M0 / pre-M2 | M2 | Change |
|---|---|---|---|
| seq_read | 2.19 MiB/s | **16.31–17.82 MiB/s** | **7.4–8.1x** |
| seq_write | 3.16 MiB/s | **4.20–4.21 MiB/s** | 1.3x |
| create | 50.6 ops/s | **67.3 ops/s** | 1.3x |
| unlink | 2613 ops/s | 405 ops/s | **6.4x slower** |
| sync | 109 774 µs | **17 503 µs** | **6.3x faster** |
| cache block | 512 B | **4 KiB** | 8x |
| cache footprint | 1024 x 512 B = 512 KiB (hardcoded) | **512 x 4 KiB = 2 MiB** (from RAM: 511 MiB usable, clamp 512..2048) | derived |
| device commands merged | — | **merged=121-126** | coalescing works |

**The plan asked for 2x sequential read; this is 7.4x**, and it came from
three separate effects that had to all be right:

1. one device command per 4 KiB block instead of one per 512-byte sector;
2. `bc_get_many` — a sequential run is fetched in ONE command (a 16 KiB read
   is one command, not four; the host test asserts this);
3. readahead on small reads, so the next block is already resident.

`sync` fell 6.3x because a flush is now 4 KiB per command *and* adjacent dirty
blocks merge into one transfer (256 KiB maximum). `seq_write` moved less
because the write path is still store-into-cache; the win there is in the
flush, which is where `sync` measures.

**`unlink` is 6.4x SLOWER (2613 -> 405 ops/s) and that is an honest
regression, not noise.** The 4 KiB block means every directory-entry update
now pulls a whole 4 KiB block through `bc_get` instead of a 512-byte sector,
and unlink touches the FAT and the directory per file. It is recorded here
rather than hidden because M6 is where the write path gets fixed; if it is
still 405 ops/s at the end of M6, M6 failed.

### /data — the CoW persistent volume (AHCI, own 64 MiB disk) — FSMODERN M1

| Metric | Value |
|---|---|
| seq_write | **0.01 MiB/s** |
| seq_read | **0.29 MiB/s** |
| create | **2.4 ops/s** |
| unlink | **62.7 ops/s** |
| sync | **184 130 µs** (184 ms) |
| payload | 6 × 4 KiB = 24 KiB, verified |

### diskfs — `/disk` (persistent, AHCI, 64 MiB image)

| Metric | Value |
|---|---|
| seq_write | **1.15 MiB/s** |
| seq_read | **5.12 MiB/s** |
| create | **295 ops/s** |
| unlink | **7 313 ops/s** |
| sync | **14 930 µs** |
| payload | 4 × 4 KiB = 16 KiB, verified |

---

## 3. What these numbers actually say

### 3.0 `/data` is 500× slower per create than tmpfs, and that is the finding

`create` on `/data` measures **2.4 ops/s** against tmpfs's 4 348 and diskfs's
295. A single `sync` costs **184 ms** for 24 KiB. Reading back the same 24 KiB
runs at 0.29 MiB/s against tmpfs's 36.55.

This is not a surprise, and it is not a regression — it is the first
measurement of a filesystem whose durability was never priced:

- every write is **copy-on-write with a SHA-256 trailer per node**, so a
  4 KiB file costs a data block, a tree node, a rewritten tree root and a
  superblock update, each checksummed;
- the tree walk is **linear in the item count** and re-reads nodes from the
  block layer with no node cache of its own;
- there is no write coalescing at the tree level at all: N items touched in a
  burst means N tree rewrites.

**This is what M6 exists to fix**, and having the number is what makes M6
falsifiable. The stated target, recorded now so it cannot be quietly moved:
`create ≥ 50 ops/s` and `sync ≤ 20 ms` for this workload, i.e. a 20× and 9×
improvement, or AuraFS is not a flagship.

`/data` being slow is *acceptable today* for exactly one reason: it is the
only filesystem in this tree that keeps its promise across a power-off, and
`/home` does not live on it yet (HOME_PLAN H4 is gated behind M3).

### 3.1 The persistent path is ~15× slower than the in-memory one

`16.98 → 1.15 MiB/s` on write, `36.55 → 5.12 MiB/s` on read. Some of that gap
is honest (a disk write must reach the device, an in-memory write need not),
but the size of it is the diagnosis: **`sync` on `/disk` costs 14.9 ms for
16 KiB**, against 1.3 ms for 32 KiB on tmpfs. That is ~30× more per KiB, and
it is where M2's write-coalescing work has to show up.

### 3.2 `create` is far more expensive than `unlink`

295 vs 7 313 ops/s on `/disk` — a factor of 25. `unlink` is cheap because
diskfs only rewrites a table entry; `create` has to find a slot, allocate,
and write. Whatever it does per create, it does ~25 times more of it than per
unlink.

### 3.3 These numbers are a *floor*, not a verdict

Every one of them runs under TCG, where a `memcpy` costs roughly what a
syscall costs on real hardware. The purpose is the **ratio between later and
earlier runs of the same lane**, and the ratchet M2 will apply to it.

---

## 4. Three findings M0 produced before it produced any number

These are the reason M0 was worth doing even if the table above were empty.

### 4.1 `bc_evict()` does not actually evict (a real block-layer defect)

`kernel/fs/buffer_cache.c`: `bc_evict()` frees a buffer by setting
`block_num = (uint64_t)-1` but leaves it **linked in the LRU list**. Calling it
in a loop therefore frees the same buffer over and over:

```
measured: 4096 bc_evict() calls, then a full re-read
          -> 204 cache hits, 0 misses
```

The cache never empties, so there is no way to force a cold read through the
public API. This is a defect of the block layer, not of any filesystem, and it
is recorded for **M2** rather than worked around.

### 4.2 diskfs has no cold path at all, by construction

diskfs's whole volume is `8 slots × 32 sectors × 512 B = 128 KiB`. The buffer
cache is `1024 × 512 B = 512 KiB`. **The entire filesystem fits in cache four
times over**, so once warm, diskfs never reads the disk again. No cold-read
throughput can be measured for it — not because the harness is weak, but
because the object does not have that property. The host lane asserts this
(`reread_misses == 0`) instead of inventing a number.

### 4.3 The first in-guest run reported `31 250 MiB/s` — and it was a lie

The first version of `tools/fsbench/fsbench.c` timed its phases with
`clock_gettime(CLOCK_MONOTONIC)`. On this tree that clock is PIT-driven at
**99 Hz**: `kernel_clock_gettime()` reads `timer_get_ticks()`, and one tick is
10.1 ms. A 32 KiB run finishes **inside one tick**, so every delta was zero
and the receipt read:

```
[fsbench] seq_write=31250.00 MiB/s
[fsbench] sync=0 us
```

That is arithmetic on a zero divisor presented as a fast filesystem — exactly
the class of claim this plan exists to prevent. It was caught by the in-guest
gate, not by the host lane (which uses the host's own microsecond clock and
was therefore fine).

**Fixed** by timing with `RDTSC`. `CR4.TSD` is not set anywhere in the tree
(`paging.c` sets SMEP/SMAP/OSFXSR and never TSD), so ring 3 may read the TSC.
The tool calibrates against the tick clock and **prints which clock it used**;
a reader must never have to guess whether a number is real.

## 5. How this table gets updated

Every phase of `FSMODERN_PLAN.md` that touches the storage stack re-runs
`bash tests/integration/cases/test_fsbench.sh` and appends a **dated row** —
never edits the old one. A performance claim without a date is folklore; that
is the whole premise of the plan.

| Date | Phase | Lane | seq_write | seq_read | create | sync | Commit |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 2026-11-22 | M0 | tmpfs | 16.98 MiB/s | 36.55 MiB/s | 4 348 ops/s | 1 303 µs | `bcc248f`+H0 |
| 2026-11-22 | M0 | diskfs | 1.15 MiB/s | 5.12 MiB/s | 295 ops/s | 14 930 µs | `bcc248f`+H0 |
| 2026-11-22 | M1 | /data (CoW) | 0.01 MiB/s | 0.29 MiB/s | 2.4 ops/s | 184 130 µs | M1 |

**What M2 must beat:** diskfs `seq_write ≥ 2.3 MiB/s` and `sync ≤ 7.5 ms` for
the same workload — i.e. a 2× improvement, or M2 does not ship.

---

## 6. What is NOT measured yet (and is named, not hidden)

| Missing | Why | Who |
|---|---|---|
| `/fat` numbers (still) | FAT32 needs its own disk and a formatted image; the case attaches one AHCI disk and `/disk` takes it. A second disk lane is M1's work. | M1 |
| Large-file throughput | diskfs caps files at 16 KiB, so no filesystem a user would call "big" exists on the default boot yet. | M1/M6 |
| Mount time | the case times the shell to prompt elsewhere (`[perf] boot-to-shell`); per-filesystem mount time is not instrumented. | M2 |
| Random 4 KiB read | the host lane measures it (`~130 000 ops/s` against a RAM device); in-guest it is dominated by the same TCG cost as sequential and adds no signal until the cache is bigger than the volume. | M2 |
| Real SSD behaviour | no hardware in this environment. | named limitation |


## M5 validation — 2026-11-24 (local continuation of `2ecdb6e`)

Measured with `tests/integration/cases/test_dir_scale.sh`, QEMU 10.0.13 TCG,
qemu64, 2 vCPUs, 512 MiB RAM, 256 MiB AHCI `/data` disk; fast boot selftests.
These conditions differ from the M0 baseline: do not infer throughput gains
from this lookup-only table.

| Names in directory | stat lookups | Passes | Measured ops/s |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| 64 | 320 | 5 | 2747.9 |
| 256 | 768 | 3 | 2948.4 |
| 1024 | 1024 | 1 | 2484.8 |

Small/large lookup-time ratio: **1.11x for 16x names** (gate <3.0x).
Final persisted geometry: depth 2, 85 leaves, 2698 items (includes directory
records, inode records and tombstones). Gate: 9/9 assertions.

Scope: `--scale` creates **empty files** and times stat, including path
formatting and syscalls. `--size 512` is accepted but does not mean 512-byte
payloads were written. This is a warm, single-run metadata measurement,
not proof of asymptotic complexity, cold-cache speed, real SSD performance,
or the M6 flagship throughput claim. No speedup against M0 is claimed here.

Before collision handling, this same workload failed to stat
`/data/s2/f_594.dat`: different names with the same 16-bit hash overwrote one
another. The repaired format uses upper key bits as collision-chain indices;
deletions leave tombstones. Host tests cover collision-head deletion and
2500-key growth to depth >=3. The on-disk 28-byte item layout and checksum
trailer stay unchanged. Previously lost entries cannot be recovered by the
patch. Chain limit: 4096; tombstone/CoW block reclamation remains future work.
